summary:
Mato Grosso do Sul stands under Brazil's uniform national framework, and the sources in this inventory identify no state-specific statute, court ruling or enforcement pattern that differentiates the state for a visitor. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since May 2013, adopted through National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013, which binds every civil registry in the country after a 14-1 vote; adoption rights followed in 2015, and lesbian, gay and bisexual people serve openly in the armed forces.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court ruled that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity constitutes a crime equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. That ruling supplies the explicit national discrimination protection that had no dedicated statute before it, and it applies on the same terms in Campo Grande as in any other Brazilian city.

Brazil has no standalone federal anti-discrimination statute, and repeal efforts have been tabled in Congress, so the protection a visitor relies on rests on the constitutional and criminal provisions as the courts read them rather than on a single consolidated law. Outright International's 2026 status review records this framework as applying uniformly across all Brazilian states.

Two gaps sit inside the framework. Intersex people in Brazil have no specific legal protections, and the Superior Court of Justice's 2023 decision permitting nonbinary people to amend their civil records shapes what a visitor's documents may show at entry, in hotels and in any interaction where identity papers are checked.
tangentialFactors:
The protection is judicially constructed rather than statutory. Because no federal anti-discrimination law exists, the reach of SOGI protection depends on how courts apply the 2019 Supreme Federal Court ruling and Lei 7.716/1989, and Congress has carried repeal efforts that keep the underlying basis contestable.

Intersex visitors fall outside the protection architecture that covers sexual orientation and gender identity, since the sources record no specific intersex protections in Brazilian law.

The 2023 recognition of nonbinary civil-record amendments is national, so documents presented by a visitor may not correspond to the binary markers assumed by routine identity checks, including border stamps, hotel registration and police identification procedures.
localsOnly:
Residents of Mato Grosso do Sul share the national framework without state variation: marriage and adoption rights since 2013 and 2015 respectively, anti-discrimination protection as a crime equivalent to racism since June 2019, and open service in the armed forces for lesbian, gay and bisexual personnel.

Since 2023 Brazilian residents have been able to amend civil records to reflect a nonbinary identity through the Superior Court of Justice's decision, which governs registry practice in the state.

Because Brazil has no consolidated federal anti-discrimination statute, residents bringing a complaint proceed under Lei 7.716/1989 and the constitutional provisions as interpreted since 2019, and Congress retains repeal efforts that could alter that footing.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory reports documented incidents of violence against trans people, police conduct, detention placement or facility access within Mato Grosso do Sul itself; the state-level risk picture is therefore unresolved on this evidence rather than established as low.

Whether interior cities in Mato Grosso do Sul differ from Campo Grande in practice, or whether any state-level policy on LGBTI detention placement exists beyond National Council of Justice Resolution 348 and Resolution 366, is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

Intersex-specific protections are recorded as absent nationally, but the sources do not describe how that gap is handled by state services in Mato Grosso do Sul.
